title: Resource-Based Authorization
description: Apply resource-based authorization for entity-level security where access depends on the specific resource being accessed.

data.text: **Resource-Based Authorization** is the pattern where access to a resource depends on the specific resource instance, not just the user's roles or claims. For example, a user should be able to edit their own documents but not documents owned by other users. This is also known as **entity-level authorization**.

data.title: Common Scenarios
items: A user can edit only their own blog posts
A manager can view reports for their department only
A project owner can invite members to their project
A support agent can access tickets assigned to them
A tenant can access only their organization's data in multi-tenant apps

data.text: ASP.NET Core provides `IAuthorizationService` for imperative authorization checks inside your code. You pass both the user and the resource to `AuthorizeAsync`, which evaluates the appropriate policy or requirement against that specific resource instance.

data.title: Document Owner Authorization

data.text: Resource handlers inherit from `AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement, TResource>`. The `TResource` is the type of the resource you're authorizing. In the handler, you have access to both the user and the specific resource instance, enabling rich authorization logic.

data.title: Document Owner Requirement and Handler
Always Load the Resource First
data.text: In resource-based authorization, you must fetch the resource from the database before calling AuthorizeAsync. Never rely on an ID parameter alone - always verify the resource exists and load it with proper includes to avoid null reference exceptions.

In multi-tenant applications, resource authorization often involves checking both ownership and tenant membership. A user might belong to Organization A and should never access Organization B's data, even if they guess a valid document ID.

data.title: Multi-Tenant Authorization Handler

data.text: In React, you typically perform resource-based authorization after fetching data. The server is the ultimate authority, but you can improve UX by hiding UI elements before the API call completes. Use route guards and conditional rendering based on resource attributes returned from the API.

data.title: Resource Authorization in React

data.text: Resource-based authorization checks are not typically cached because the resource state can change. However, for read-heavy scenarios, you can cache the authorization result with a short TTL or use a cache-aside pattern. Never cache authorization decisions longer than the resource's expected mutation interval.

data.title: Avoid N+1 Authorization Queries
data.text: When authorizing lists of resources (e.g., 'show all documents the user can edit'), avoid running individual authorization checks per item. Use a single query with WHERE clauses that incorporate the user's permissions.

data.caption: Resource-based authorization flow for document editing
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant A as API Controller
    participant DB as Database
    participant Auth as AuthService
    C->>A: PUT /documents/123
    A->>DB: Load document 123
    DB-->>A: Document {id: 123, OwnerId: "user-42"}
    A->>Auth: AuthorizeAsync(User, document, "CanEdit")
    Auth->>Auth: Check OwnerId == User.Id
    alt Authorized
        Auth-->>A: Success
        A->>DB: Save changes
        A-->>C: 204 No Content
    else Not Authorized
        Auth-->>A: Forbidden
        A-->>C: 403 Forbidden
    end

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Resource-based authorization checks specific resource instances
Use IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync with a resource parameter
Handlers can access the resource via generic TResource parameter
Always load the resource before authorizing
Multi-tenant apps require additional tenant validation
data.takeaway: Resource-based authorization is essential for entity-level security in multi-user applications.
